# Beginnings

Starting a process, a workflow of thinking, about a controversial idea is time consuming and frustrating.  

There are a host of psychological obstacles to just get going.  

tip:  notice when you start to tune out of your work, when you go to your phone to "self medicate" on social media:  What were you just reading before that?  What did your mind do before you grabbed a distraction device?  Track those things because you might discover an edge for you in regards to intellectual work. 


So, when you start this work, begin with some acceptance that you'll encounter blockages, frustrations, dead ends. Brute forcing your way through will not typically lead to satisfaction.  


I'm not sure the best way to think about it, to be honest. I usually find mysefl working in spurts...I'll have a lot of motivation and emotion, will get through it, and then have to just stop.  

I think this is normal.  I think it's common.  

Tip: have a system to track your progress so that when you come back to this work (next week, month, whenever), you don't waste a lot of time getting caught up to speed. call out to niklas lumen


# Identifying the claim

Sometimes it's not obvious.  Sometimes claims are implicit.   And that means time spent getting the claim out is worthwhile.

## Example

As an example, consider the claim that new gun laws should not be allowed because laws won't stop gun violence. 

<!-- On the one hand, there is a clear claim about gun laws, but what is implicit might be more important: -->

Since laws can't prevent 100% of undesirable behavior then we should not enact the law.

This is a type of false dichotomy.  If a law isn't 100% effective we should do nothing.

That's implied and not obvious.

Being able to detect those sort of things take time, practice, and expertise. My example is somewhat advanced.

## Beginning with a claim


Don't let this turn into a quick splattering of whatever you think of. 

Let me try to start with something that has gotten me piqued:  trans-girls in girl highschool sports.

There is a huge amount of issues wrapped in this topic.  At first it might seem simple but there are nuances. 


# Where to begin

What is implicit in the claim that girls who've transitioned should not participate in cis-girl sports (notice I'm adding cis as a way to increase precision)?

Make a list of what is going on, just for starters:

1. trans-girls are stronger
2. trans-girls are faster
3. trans-girls have more muscle/bone density

Notice that I'm avoiding some moral questions about treating different groups of people differently. 

That would create other sets of questions.  Valid questions. But often it is useful to think about non-moral issues first because of practical needs.   For example, I might believe that pedestrians should 100% of the time be safe to walk on sidewalks, crosswalks, or even streets. But how likely will 100% be attained?  I think we should have policy that leads to harm reduction, which might include things like streets designed for slower speeds, traffic cameras around intersections and dangerous streets, perhaps even engine governors that prevent high speeds. But it's unlikely to prevent 100% of pedestrian injuries.


So I'm wanting to point out that maybe we can avoid the "shoulds" and "oughts" about controversial ideas and shifting towards something that can be quantified. 

## Constellation of issues

Back to the list that I've started:

1. trans-girls are stronger
2. trans-girls are faster
3. trans-girls have more muscle/bone density

I hope at this point you might be recognizing that these questions represent a sort of semantic constellation of ideas. 

```{r,echo=F}
sports <- dagitty("dag{
                   transgirls -> stronger
                   transgirls -> faster
                   transgirls -> more_dense}
                   ")

plot(sports)

```

For now I'm going to pivot towards something I very much want students to appreciate:

Compared to what?  trans-girls are stronger compared to what? 

## Compared to what?

This is question that is actually an intellectual super-power.  Because it has the ability to frame your thinking, the thinking of others.  

And it's hard to find the right comparison.  There may be many comparisons.
